Hasinai

Hasinai is a historical Caddo community grouping associated with East Texas, rather than a separate present-day government in this directory. Caddo historian Cecile Elkins Carter’s account distinguishes Hasinai from other named Caddo branches. Selected Hasinai-specific scholarship and a public historic-site history supply additional regional context while leaving the underlying records open.

Read the sources [1] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [2] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Names, river valleys and communities

Carter places Hasinai communities in East Texas within a wider Caddo history, while Magnaghi’s reference entry locates them in the middle Neches and upper Angelina valleys. The latter describes agricultural hamlets encountered in the seventeenth century. Read these accounts with their different perspectives and periods visible. A historical grouping, a linguistic family and a modern government are different kinds of relationship; the sources do not establish that every Caddo person or archaeological site is specifically Hasinai.

Read the sources [1] Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter [2] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

02

Place interpretation and later movement

The Caddo Mounds site history discusses Hasinai communities continuing in East Texas through the 1830s and later Caddo displacement toward the Brazos. This supplies the bridge to the modern museum exterior used here. The photograph is a public interpretation institution in the related region, not a historical Hasinai house or a proof of direct subgroup identity for ancient mound builders. Sensitive burial and ceremonial descriptions, cultural rankings and unreviewed archaeological conclusions are excluded from this introduction.

Read the sources [3] Texas Historical Commission [2] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

Caddo Homeland ↗

Cecile Elkins Carter, an enrolled Caddo historian, presents a Caddo-centered synthesis using oral history, archival records, and historical group names. The page distinguishes broad Caddo use from the narrower historical Cadohadacho label; these are attributed historical interpretations rather than a universal current naming rule.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: The full visible page and the separate credits page were read. Its account is Carter’s researched and written synthesis; underlying cited archives and all referenced books were not independently reviewed.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

https://www.texasbeyondhistory.net/tejas/voices/images/homeland.html

Hasinai Indians — selected historical and regional passages ↗

Publication: Undated publication

Russell M. Magnaghi’s entry provides specifically Hasinai naming, river-valley and settlement context. Selected historical paragraphs are read with Carter’s Caddo-centered account. The article’s dated cultural rankings, ceremonial/burial descriptions and confident archaeological reconstructions are not adopted.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Selected actual main-body paragraphs, web lines 7–10, 14–15 and 18–19, plus author and bibliography read. Synthesis uses East Texas Neches/Angelina context, agricultural hamlets and later movement only. Ceremonial details, burial material, evaluative cultural rankings, ancient identity equivalence, exact community counts and current descendant assertions excluded. Underlying bibliography not read.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body readable without an account in this inspection. Linked bibliography, archival instruments and media remain separate works unless expressly listed.

https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/hasinai-indians

Caddo Mounds History ↗

A site history summarizes the settlement and ceremonial center at Caddo Mounds and later Hasinai and Caddo movement. Its account is useful for this particular site and institutional chronology, not a complete history of the Caddo people.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: The full visible history article and its listed chronology were read. Interpretations of why the center was vacated remain attributed to the site’s archaeological account.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

https://thc.texas.gov/state-historic-sites/caddo-mounds/caddo-mounds-history
